primary_topics: Tone-setting keynote at the GAJE (Global Alliance of Justice Education) 5th Worldwide Conference held in the Philippines, December 8, 2008
Obama's victory as a milestone in the global battle for human dignity and equality -- from Magna Carta to French Revolution to American Bill of Rights to the Philippines

Two conference projects proposed: (1) International Criminal Court (Rome Statute 1998; effective 2002; four crime categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, crime of aggression); (2) PERLAS -- Public Education on the Rule of Law (pearl of great price in Filipino and Spanish; workbooks for elementary and high schools already developed)
New paradigms of justice: mediation instead of litigation; public interest law centers; international bridges to justice; independent human rights commissions; writs of amparo; ICC; PERLAS
sub_topics: Obama victory: 'a major milestone in the battle for human dignity and equality that started with the adoption of the Magna Charta by the British, carried on by all independence-loving peoples everywhere, to the French Revolution, and then to America where the ideals of human freedom were immortalized in the Bill of Rights of the American Constitution'

Philippine constitutional heritage: all Philippine Constitutions enshrine the Bill of Rights; the Constitution also contains a Declaration of State Policies mandating 'a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty'; Congress has passed various social justice measures

ICC origin: founded July 17, 1998 when 120 states signed the Rome Statute at the Rome Diplomatic Conference; became effective July 1, 2002 when 60 of the 120 ratified; sanctions violations of International Humanitarian Law (armed conflicts) and International Human Rights Law (peacetime)

ICC mandate: fight the impunity of dictators, presidents and heads of state who 'could not be sued in their home countries due to their national immunity from suit' for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression

PERLAS: Public Education on the Rule of Law; 'PERLAS, which in Filipino and Spanish means a pearl of great price, was conceived and born'; idea is to teach basics of democracy, rule of law, justice and peace at basic schools; workbooks and teaching exemplars already developed and printed, ready for use in Philippine elementary and high schools

Rule of law as the solution: 'in many places in the world, we still have rulers or leaders who believe and practice authoritarianism in various forms. On the opposite extreme, are regimes where mobs and charlatans abuse democratic processes and defy constitutions. The solution to both these extremes is the rule of law. No one should be so powerful, so moneyed or so influential as to be above the law.'

New paradigm enumeration: 'mix these mantras with the cyber-age concepts of globalization and high-tech education, and we come face to face with new paradigms of justice like mediation in lieu of litigation, public interest law centers, international bridges to justice, independent commissions on human rights, writs of amparo and, if I may be allowed to stress, the International Criminal Court and PERLAS, the pearl of a great price'

stances.claim: The ICC is the most significant new paradigm of international justice because it directly addresses the impunity of heads of state -- those who 'could not be sued in their home countries due to their national immunity from suit.' By making genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression internationally prosecutable, it closes the accountability gap that national courts cannot fill.
stances.rhetorical_move: impunity-gap argument: the ICC as the specific institutional solution to the specific problem of national immunity for heads of state
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing justification for the ICC

stances.claim: PERLAS -- teaching the basics of democracy, rule of law, justice and peace at the elementary and high school level -- is the most foundational educational reform possible: it builds the civic knowledge base that all other reforms depend on. Workbooks already developed and ready for deployment makes this immediately actionable, not merely aspirational.
stances.rhetorical_move: foundational-education argument: rule-of-law education at the basic school level as the prerequisite for all other governance reforms
stances.confidence: asserted as an immediately actionable proposal

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered December 8, 2008 as the tone-setting keynote at the GAJE (Global Alliance of Justice Education) 5th Worldwide Conference in the Philippines, this address by CJP opens with Obama's election as 'a major milestone in the battle for human dignity and equality that started with the adoption of the Magna Charta by the British, carried on by all independence-loving peoples, to the French Revolution, and then to America where human freedom was immortalized in the Bill of Rights.' He situates the Philippines in this history (all Constitutions enshrine the Bill of Rights; the Constitution mandates 'a just and dynamic social order to free the people from poverty'). He proposes two projects for the GAJE conference: (1) The ICC -- founded July 17, 1998 (120 states at the Rome Diplomatic Conference; effective July 1, 2002 with 60 ratifications); fights the impunity of dictators and heads of state 'who could not be sued in their home countries due to national immunity from suit' for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. (2) PERLAS (Public Education on the Rule of Law) -- 'which in Filipino and Spanish means a pearl of great price'; teaches the basics of democracy, rule of law, justice and peace at the basic school level; workbooks and teaching exemplars already developed and printed, ready for Philippine elementary and high schools. The governing political philosophy: 'in many places, we still have rulers who practice authoritarianism... on the opposite extreme, regimes where mobs and charlatans abuse democratic processes. The solution to both extremes is the rule of law. No one should be so powerful, so moneyed or so influential as to be above the law.' He closes with a new-paradigm enumeration: 'mix these mantras with the cyber-age and globalization, and we come face to face with new paradigms of justice like mediation in lieu of litigation, public interest law centers, international bridges to justice, independent commissions on human rights, writs of amparo and, if I may stress, the International Criminal Court and PERLAS, the pearl of a great price.'
